1:
The two names at the head of the chapter are Babylonian, and the voices spend some care on them. John Gill takes Bel to be the Belus of the Babylonians, a renowned king deified after his death, who walled Babylon about and had a temple there with gates of brass still standing in the time of Herodotus; the name is taken up into their kings, as in Belshazzar. Nebo he makes an oracular idol, named from a root meaning to prophesy, answering to the Apollo or Mercury of other nations, and he notes that the Alexandrian copy of the Septuagint wrongly puts Dagon in its place. Matthew Henry reaches the same result by another road: Bel a deified prince, Nebo a deified prophet, for so the word signifies, so that the pair were the Jupiter and the Mercury of Babylon. John Wesley agrees that profane historians call the first Jupiter Belus and the second delivered oracles. Charles Ellicott looks to the monuments instead and makes Bel perhaps identical with Marduk, and Nabu, the Revealer, a kind of Assyrian Hermes.

Henry sets the scene as a conqueror’s inventory. It was usual to destroy the gods of a conquered people and put your own in their room, and when Cyrus takes Babylon the idols that were set up on high, bold and erect, shall stoop at the feet of the soldiers plundering their temples. The gold and silver laid on them to adorn them serves only to expose them; they are loaded on the carriers’ horses and sent into Persia among other lumber, for so it seems the plunderers accounted them rather than treasure. John Calvin presses the same picture harder: the robbers shall collect into one large heap the gods that formerly occupied an elevated station, and shall huddle them together on waggons without any respect, as the waggoners think proper. He grants that this was fulfilled when the Persians and Medes took Babylon by storm, but holds that Isaiah looked farther, to the coming of Christ, whose brightness leaves no room for false gods at all.

Ellicott alone raises a difficulty from outside the text. An inscription lately deciphered presents the conqueror in another aspect altogether: in it he describes himself as a worshipper of Bel and Nebo, and prays to them for length of days. Ellicott canvasses the ways of reconciling the two. We may say that the prophet idealises the policy and character of the king; or that the monotheistic element which appears in his treatment of the Jews was after all dominant, in spite of episodes like the one the inscription indicates; or that the recognition of the Babylonian deities followed on the submission of the people and was preceded by some rougher treatment. What the contrast makes probable, he adds, is that the prophecy was not written after the inscription.

Adam Clarke works on the words. He renders the clause about the carriages as burdens that are heavy, the Greek translators having read a suffix meaning their rather than your; and at the second verse he takes what the idols could not deliver to be their own charge, that is, their worshippers, who ought to have been borne by them. The Chaldee and Syriac come to the same purpose, though he confesses he does not understand how they render the word in an active sense; and he prefers the reading with an added letter that many of the collated copies carry, as giving more elegance to the passage. Ellicott, for the moment, distinguishes the deities from their images: they are powerless to rescue them, and so far as they have any being at all, that being is itself carried away captive. Gill asks who it is that stoops, and answers that it is likelier the Babylonians themselves than either the beasts or the idols, and Wesley makes it both together, neither able to help the other.
3:
The address turns from the gods that must be carried to the God who carries, and every voice feels the force of the reversal. Charles Ellicott calls the choice of words singularly emphatic: the false gods are borne away as a burden, while the true God bears, that is, supports, his people, and every I in the sentence is emphasised in the Hebrew. Adam Clarke praises the ingenuity and force of the contrast. God like an indulgent father had carried his people in his arms as a man carries his son, protecting them and delivering them out of their distresses, whereas the idols of the heathen must themselves be carried about and shifted from place to place with great labour and fatigue by their worshippers, and can neither answer nor deliver those who cry to them. Clarke sets beside it the complaint of Moses, who expostulated about the weight of the charge laid on him in the same image, asking whether he had conceived all this people, that he should be told to carry them in his bosom as a nursing father bears the sucking child. John Wesley keeps it domestic: God has nourished them ever since they came out of Egypt, as tenderly as parents bring up their own children. John Gill notes only that the house of Jacob means the Jews, the descendants of Jacob.

John Calvin makes the metaphor maternal rather than paternal and dwells on it. God compares himself to a mother who carries the child in her womb and afterwards carries it in her bosom, and he addresses the Jews so that they may answer out of their own experience, having felt that he bore both them and their burdens. How far the figure may be pressed Calvin leaves open. It might be taken simply of a God who nourished that people like a newborn infant; but since he also begat them spiritually, Calvin does not object to extending the words to mean that they were brought out of the bowels of God into a new life and the hope of an eternal inheritance.

He raises the obvious objection against himself: God is everywhere called a Father, and that title is the more appropriate one. His answer is that no figure of speech can describe the affection of God toward us, which is infinite and various, so that if all that can be said or imagined about love were gathered into one it would still be surpassed. On the word remnant he is bleak. The greater part had been alienated from the Church by their revolt, so that the hope of deliverance belonged to a very small number only; and since unbelievers were as deaf as the heathen nations, a hearing has to be demanded of them.

At the fourth verse the voices divide over a single word. Calvin thinks the Hebrew term rendered he very emphatic, where some interpreters give it flatly as the demonstrative pronoun; on his reading it means that God is always the same and like himself, not only in his essence but with respect to us, so that we ourselves feel him to be the same. Gill says the same without the grammar: the same he ever was in love and sympathy, in power and protection, in promise and faithfulness, in the last days of his people as at the first moment of their conversion. Ellicott marks where the human comparison breaks off, since the care of a mother ceases in the natural course of things before a man grows old, while this care endures to the end of life. Calvin meets one more objection here, that it seems absurd for men who ought to grow up to be carried still; but examine it properly, he answers, and we never make such progress that we do not need upholding, for otherwise the most perfect man would stumble every moment.
5:
The challenge of the fifth verse is met with two different accounts of what it attacks. Matthew Henry calls the thing absurd twice over: absurd to represent an infinite and eternal Spirit by the figure of any creature, which changes his truth into a lie and turns his glory into shame; and absurd again to set any creature level with the Creator, because between infinite and finite there is no proportion. John Gill asks whether among all the angels of heaven or the sons of men there is any to whom such a God could be likened. Charles Ellicott notes that the argument is renewed here in nearly its old form, and that the fate of Bel and Nebo is being urged against those who thought they might worship Jehovah in the way those deities had been worshipped; the calves at Bethel and at Dan were that sin, and so, he adds, was carrying the ark into battle against the Philistines.

John Calvin objects that this reading is too small. Many commentators, he says, have absurdly weakened the statement by supposing that the prophet merely attacks superstitious persons who ascribe divine power to wood or stone. What is reproved, he has no doubt, is the conclusion the people drew under adversity: seeing the Babylonians prosper, they imagined God favourable to them, which would mean that he approves of idolatry, and so his honour would be conveyed to dumb creatures. The remedy is not to estimate the power of God by the present state of things.

On the making of the idol the voices agree and divide the labour between them. Gill pictures the rich man giving his gold profusely to a workman without caring what it costs, and remembers the image sixty cubits high and six broad. Calvin finds two fathers of such a god, the rich man who lavishes the metal and the workman who adds the shape, and fastens on the suddenness of the change: they bow before the metal the moment it has taken a form regulated by their own caprice. A particle, he thinks, heightens the madness, since there might be room for repentance in a man overtaken by a sudden mistake, whereas these persevere obstinately. Henry turns it against the reader. The profuseness of idolaters shames the niggardliness of many who call themselves servants of God but want a religion that costs them nothing; and while some lavish gold out of the bag to make an idol in the house, others hoard gold in the bag to make an idol in the heart, covetousness being idolatry too, as dangerous though not as scandalous.

At the seventh verse Henry keeps the procession comic and pitiful at once: they carry him on their own shoulders and hire no porters, they set him on his pedestal more like a dead corpse than a living God, and they take great pains to fasten him so that they may always know where to find him, knowing all the while that he can neither move a hand nor stir a step. Adam Clarke says the description is so exact a picture of an idolatrous procession he had read of among the Hindoos that the prophet might almost be supposed to have been sitting among them, and he brings in Pindar, who was told that a brazen statue could be had for the price of his ode, and answered that he was no maker of statues to stand for ever on one base, his song going out instead to distant realms. He notes too that Jeremiah seems indebted to this passage. Keil and Delitzsch read the following call as a second admonition, addressed now to those who would imitate the heathen, and take the thing to be remembered to be the nothingness of idols; the verb that follows it they leave contested between playing the man and being made strong.
8:
The verb rendered shew yourselves men is a word that occurs nowhere else, and the chapter’s longest dispute gathers on it. Adam Clarke calls its derivation and signification doubtful and reports that the old translators seem to have read something different: one gives take shame to yourselves, another consider with yourselves, a third a word for mourning. Charles Ellicott keeps the received sense but reads it as irony, the worshippers of idols being told they should at least have the courage of their convictions, and notes that a conjectural emendation yields the opposite meaning, be ye deeply ashamed. John Calvin canvasses the derivations one by one: some take it from the word for man and render act a manly part, others from a word meaning foundation and render take courage, while Jerome derives it from the word for fire, which Calvin thinks the more appropriate when a people’s disgrace has just been exposed. He settles for being ashamed, but leaves it to every person to form his own judgment. He also prefers to render the next clause return to the heart rather than recall, which he calls feeble, since forgetfulness of the benefits of God is a sort of madness; and Keil and Delitzsch note how much that word carries, everything the Greek terms distribute among mind, reason, conscience and spirit is gathered in Hebrew into the heart. Calvin asks besides whether the verse addresses Jews or Gentiles, and though he grants that every man has some seed of religion by nature, the context decides him for the Jews.

The proofs that follow are handled briskly. John Gill fills out the former things with the creation of heaven and earth, the destruction of the old world, the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah, and the bringing of Israel out of Egypt through the Red sea. Ellicott works on the two names, the first meaning the mighty and strong one, the second the one true object of worship, and observes that what follows asserts what we should call omniscience and omnipotence. Calvin presses the exclusiveness: God wishes not merely to be acknowledged but to be alone acknowledged, since if he admitted any companion his throne would shake, for either there is one God or there is none at all. John Wesley adds that the foretelling runs from the beginning of the world to the end of it.

Who the ravenous bird is the voices settle almost together. Gill reports that some made it Abraham and some Nebuchadnezzar, and rejects both for Cyrus, adding that the word denotes swiftness rather than rapacity, that Xenophon notes how Cyrus urged dispatch on his soldiers, that Tigranes told him he had come with a great army from a far country before the other could gather his own, and that Cyrus wished to be reckoned a winged man. Clarke renders it the eagle and observes that the ensign of Cyrus was a golden eagle, the Greek word for it standing about as near the Hebrew as Greek letters allow. Ellicott adds that the standard was borne by his successors too, and identifies the sun-rising as Persia and the far country probably as Media.

Calvin alone declines the bird. He grants that most interpreters render the word a bird of prey and that this is its true signification, but chooses instead a sense he finds among some Hebrew writers, by which it stands for thought or decree, so that the man of counsel in the next clause becomes a repetition of it rather than a new figure. He turns the alternative over before leaving it: if the bird is kept, the metaphor is beautiful, Cyrus falling on Babylon so suddenly that he seemed to fly, and the prophet may even be glancing at the auguries the Babylonians were addicted to, who watched the flight of birds for knowledge of the future and did not foresee this one.
12:
The last summons is addressed to the stouthearted, and the voices cannot agree who they are. Adam Clarke takes it briefly for the Babylonians, stubbornly bent on injustice toward the Israelites. John Gill knows that reading, attributes it to Kimchi and others, and rejects it outright: the address is to the Jews themselves, or at least to the wicked among them, who were always a stiffnecked people, while even those who made more pretences to religion were merely self-righteous. He then widens it past the nation to all who are stubborn of heart, proud of their wisdom and strength, some of them so daring as to make a mock at sin and outbrave death itself. John Calvin is with Gill on the persons and harsher on the fault. The rebuke is sharp, he grants, but deserved by men whose hearts no promise and no gracious invitation could soothe. Distress had not humbled these Jews; though almost overwhelmed they swelled with pride, and having thrown off the fear of God they rose to outrageous madness, as he says still happens to many whom affliction only makes more rebellious. By murmuring and fretting, poor distressed persons shut the door against the very assistance they need. Charles Ellicott declines to name a nation and works on the word, which implies obduracy and ignorance at once, so that such men are self-excluded from the righteousness set before them.

How the following clause is to be read Calvin leaves open in two ways at once. Those called far from righteousness may be men incapable of receiving the grace of God, or Jews so wholly abandoned to crimes as to be desperate; on the second reading there is a beautiful contrast between the righteousness of men and that of God. He offers a further alternative on the word itself, that it may stand for the assistance of God as it does in the next verse, and says only that whoever prefers it may enjoy his opinion, since it is not inappropriate. What he will not allow is that unbelief settles the matter. It is a very great obstacle, but not such an obstacle as can hinder God from manifesting the power of his truth at last; and if he did not exceed the malice of men by his goodness, we should all perish without exception, for who is there that uses his grace as he ought.

He guards it immediately from being taken too widely. The prophet did not include wicked apostates among those who shall partake of the promised salvation, but says only that God has at hand a method by which his righteousness shall be made manifest; and the rebuke goes to the whole nation, both to convict the hardened and to chastise the elect, who had themselves sometimes appeared infected with the same plague. Ellicott puts the other side of it in a sentence: their unfaithfulness does not hinder the faithfulness of God, who brings his salvation near to all who are ready to receive it.

What the righteousness is divides them again. Calvin makes it the same thing as the salvation named beside it, that is, the assistance promised to the people, since the most remarkable instance of the righteousness of God is his delivering them; and the glory of God, he adds, is bound to that deliverance by an indissoluble bond. John Wesley keeps it historical, God showing himself righteous and faithful by making good his promise to deliver them out of Babylon after seventy years, and bringing his people to Zion to be his glory once again. Gill runs through four possibilities and settles on the last: the faithfulness of God, or his justice displayed in redemption, or Christ himself, or rather the righteousness of Christ imputed to believers, near in the Gospel for faith to come at, and never far off from the man to whom it is reckoned.
